title: Endurance exercise performance in Masters athletes: age-associated changes and underlying physiological mechanisms
population: Masters (older) endurance athletes; review of published studies
findings: Peak endurance performance is maintained until approximately 35 years of age, followed by modest decreases until 50-60 years, with progressively steeper declines thereafter.

A progressive reduction in VO2max appears to be the primary mechanism of the age-related decline in endurance performance; a lower lactate threshold also contributes but may be secondary to the fall in VO2max.
Exercise economy (metabolic cost of sustained submaximal exercise) does not change with age in endurance-trained adults.
Decreases in maximal stroke volume, heart rate and arterio-venous O2 difference all appear to contribute to the reduced VO2max in endurance-trained athletes.

Declines in performance and its physiological determinants appear mediated in large part by a reduction in the intensity (velocity) and volume of exercise that can be performed during training sessions.
limitations: Narrative review without systematic search; much of the underlying data are cross-sectional comparisons of different individuals at different ages. No numeric decline rates in the abstract.
implications: Age-based projection: flat to about 35, gentle decline to 50-60, steeper after; make the slope a parameter, not a constant.
Do not apply an age penalty to running-economy assumptions for trained runners; attribute projected decline to VO2max and threshold paces.
Because decline is partly mediated by the reduced intensity and volume masters can train at, do not cut quality or volume purely on age; adjust on observed tolerance, recovery and injury signals.

verification.notes: Crossref title/journal/year/first author match. Every finding matched against the Europe PMC abstract (reworded finding 1 slightly to say lactate threshold is 'also contributing').
